raw_answer_text:
A1: The clock signal toggles at a constant, regular rate throughout the diagram.
A2: All three signals (request, acknowledge, completion) rest at a low level at the start.
A3: The request signal transitions first.
A4: No, the acknowledge signal cannot assert before the request, because it is defined as a response to the request being asserted (it must follow, not precede, the request).
A5: The request signal returns low once the acknowledge signal has asserted, signaling that the requester has seen its request accepted/acted upon.
A6: The acknowledge signal returns low once the request signal has returned low (i.e., after it observes the request has been de-asserted), completing the four-phase cycle.
A7: The completion signal indicates that the requested operation/transfer has finished; it occurs after the request has been acknowledged, marking the end of the active data transfer phase within the handshake.
A8: (1) Request asserts (goes high); (2) Acknowledge asserts (goes high) in response; (3) Request de-asserts (goes low); (4) Acknowledge de-asserts (goes low), returning both signals to idle.
